All four of those rows fell to about the 40th to 50th percentile on new photos, so that pattern was most likely noise from small groups (the left-third group had only 5 to 6 photos). The unit is driven mainly by its photo classes rather than by any of the composition, lighting or color properties asked about.

At most, the unit may prefer sharp, colored images, but nothing here is confident.

null_s3.explanation: No reliable, unit-specific selectivity for these photo properties is established. In the original photos the unit appeared weaker when the main subject faced left or sat in the left third of the frame. On new photos this mostly did not replicate. The left-third comparisons rested on only 5–6 photos and reversed sign. The left-facing effect shrank to percentile 88 for camera-facing versus left, and to 60 for no clear direction versus left. A mild dislike of left-facing subjects may remain, but it is too weak to call this unit's own. The other effects shared similar units or were small and below the 95th percentile. These were lower activity on black-and-white photos (5 photos) and on blurry subjects. So this unit's activity is best explained by photo class rather than by any of the framing, lighting, color or orientation properties asked about.

null_s1.explanation: None of this unit's apparent preferences survived replication. The strongest pattern in the original photos was lower activity on left-facing subjects (rows 2–3) and on subjects centred in the left third (rows 13–15). On new photos the left-third effects vanished or reversed, though the left-third rows rest on only 5–6 photos. The facing-left effect shrank to percentile 88 for camera-facing vs left and 60 for no-direction vs left. So any dislike of left-facing subjects is weak at best. Two other effects were never tested on new photos. Lower activity on black-and-white photos rests on just 5 photos, and two of the three comparisons are at percentile 94–96. Lower activity on blurry subjects reaches only percentile 93 and is shared by a similar unit. Neither is reliable. Overall the unit is mainly driven by its photo classes, and no photographic attribute in this table can be confidently assigned to it.

null_s2.explanation: No clear, unit-specific signal survives. The strongest original effects were weaker activity for left-facing or left-placed subjects (rows 2, 3, 13, 15). All four failed on new photos, and the left-third effects even reversed, so those effects were likely noise from very small groups (5 to 6 photos). The left-facing effect in row 2 stayed positive (percentile 88) but was not unusual. The remaining hint is that the unit is weaker on black-and-white or nearly colorless photos than on tinted or normal-color ones (rows 24, 26, 27). That rests on only 5 photos, and row 27 is shared with a similar unit. There is also a mild preference for sharp over slightly blurry subjects (row 31, percentile 93). Overall the unit seems to respond weakly to color presence and image sharpness, with no reliable compositional or orientation tuning.
